review_status: DRAFT. Must be reviewed by an agricultural officer or plant pathologist before release.

disclaimer.text: This app gives a first guess from a photo and it can be wrong. It does not replace advice from an agricultural officer, a Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or ICAR-CPCRI. When you use any spray, follow the label and safety rules.

summary.text: This leaf looks healthy in the photo. No signs of Yellow Leaf Disease or leaf spot were found.

signs_to_watch.text: Yellow tips on the outer leaves, often with green stripes along the edges.
Small brown or black round spots with a yellow ring (leaf spot).
Check more often from September to November, when yellowing is easiest to see.

what_to_do.text: Keep good drainage so water does not stand around the palms.
Keep up regular fertilizer and organic manure as advised for your area.
Take a new photo if you notice any change in the leaves.

limits.text: One photo cannot show early or hidden disease. If the palm looks unwell in any way, ask an expert even if this result says healthy.

check_signs.text: Yellow leaf tips with green stripes along the edges
Small brown or black round spots with a yellow ring

summary.text: The model leans toward the healthy nut class for this photo. This is a screening suggestion; one photo cannot rule out early fruit rot.

signs_to_watch.text: A water-soaked patch near the top (calyx end) of the nut, and the nut loses its shine.
Dark green patches that spread over the nut, then the nut rots and falls.
Check after heavy rain, because the disease spreads in wet monsoon weather.

what_to_do.text: No disease-control treatment is suggested by this screening result alone. Continue your usual garden care.
Check the same bunch after prolonged wet weather, or if nuts begin to fall.
If nuts show dark, water-soaked patches, rot, or fall repeatedly, show the bunch to an agricultural officer or KVK.

limits.text: The model checks visible signs in this photo; early disease can be missed. If nuts show dark, water-soaked patches or keep falling, ask an agricultural officer or KVK to check the bunch.

ripe_note.text: Ripe nuts can be orange or yellow. Colour alone is not a sign of disease, so compare nuts that are equally ripe.

check_signs.text: A water-soaked patch near the top of the nut
Nuts that darken, rot and fall after rain

summary.text: This photo looks consistent with fruit rot of areca nut, called Mahali or Koleroga. It is a disease that spreads in wet monsoon weather and rots the nuts. Only an expert can confirm it.

what_it_means.text: Nuts get water-soaked patches, turn dark, rot and fall.
A white mould can grow on the fallen nuts.
Infected nuts usually fall without the small calyx cap at the top.
In bad cases the nut stalks are also affected.

possible_causes.text: A Phytophthora organism (Phytophthora meadii) infects the nuts.
It spreads in cool, humid weather, when heavy rain alternates with short sunny spells during the south-west monsoon.

what_to_do.text: Collect fallen and rotten nuts regularly and destroy them, for example by burning, so the disease does not spread.
Spray the bunches with 1% Bordeaux mixture as protection: first spray after the pre-monsoon showers, second spray 40 to 45 days later, and a third spray if the monsoon goes on for long.
Spray finely so the whole bunch is covered.
Covering bunches with polythene covers (125 gauge, 75 x 60 cm) also worked very well as a barrier.
Spraying after the disease is already spreading often does not control it well, so do not wait. Talk to an agricultural officer if many nuts are falling.

when_to_get_help.text: If the new spindle leaf in the crown turns yellow, then brown, or the crown looks rotten, get expert help at once. This can be bud rot or crown rot, caused by the same organism.

limits.text: This result is only a guess from one photo. Several nuts from the same bunch or garden can help the expert decide.

text.text: Young nuts and buttons can also fall because of poor pollination, lack of nutrients, water stress or heat. Look for a water-soaked patch before deciding it is Mahali.
Nuts that split at the tip are a different problem linked to growing conditions, not Mahali.

check_signs.text: A water-soaked, dark green patch on the nut, usually near the top
Nuts that rot and fall, sometimes with white mould on the fallen nut

Yellow_Leaf.display_name: Yellow leaf disease or leaf spotting (please confirm)

summary.text: This photo shows yellowing or spotting of leaves. It can be consistent with Yellow Leaf Disease. Spotted leaves can also mean a leaf spot disease, so please confirm with an expert.

what_it_means.text: Yellowing starts at the tips of the leaflets on the outer leaves and spreads along the edges, with green stripes left between.
Leaf tips dry out. Later the leaves become small, stiff and pointed, and the crown gets smaller.
The roots turn black and rot. Nuts can be small and fall early.
The signs are clearest from September to November and may fade in summer.

possible_causes.text: ICAR-CPCRI links Yellow Leaf Disease to a phytoplasma spread by a plant hopper.

The cause is not fully settled. One Indian study did not find a phytoplasma in the palms it tested, and a later study notes that similar yellowing has been linked to different pathogens in different regions.

what_to_do.text: There is no spray that cures this disease, so good care of the garden is the main defence.

Give fertilizer regularly in two splits each year. ICAR-CPCRI advises 100 g nitrogen, 40 g phosphorus and 140 g potash per palm per year, plus 800 g Mussorie phos, and 12 kg each of compost and green leaf per palm per year. Confirm current doses with your agricultural officer.
Avoid water standing in the garden by keeping good drainage, and grow cover crops between palms.
Removing badly affected palms can slow the spread.
Do not use antibiotic or insecticide sprays on your own. Some web pages list them, but ICAR-CPCRI says ordinary plant protection does not control this disease. Ask an agricultural officer first.

text.text: Small brown to black round spots with a yellow ring, mostly in the monsoon and more common on palms under 10 years old, usually on the lower leaves. A 1% Bordeaux mixture spray is listed for it.
Yellowing of the outer leaves, which then droop and fall, with a brown patch or brown ooze at the base of the trunk. This needs expert help.
The new spindle leaf in the crown turns yellow, then brown and rots, or the outer leaves yellow and dry from the base. This is urgent, so get expert help at once.

limits.text: The photos used to teach this app include spotted leaves as well as yellow leaves, so this result may mean either one. Treat it as a reason to get the palm checked.

check_signs.text: Yellow leaf tips on the outer leaves, spreading along the edges with green stripes left between
Separate brown or black round spots with a yellow ring (this points to leaf spot instead)

Photograph the same plant from another angle.

bordeaux_mixture_recipe.title: How to make 1% Bordeaux mixture (100 litres)
bordeaux_mixture_recipe.verify: The scan of source S1 is partly unclear about the lime quantity. Confirm 1 kg lime with a local agricultural officer before release.

steps.text: Dissolve 1 kg of copper sulphate in 50 litres of water.
In a separate vessel, mix 1 kg of lime in 50 litres of water.
Mix the two solutions just before spraying.
Test it: dip a polished iron knife or nail in the mixture. A brown coating means too much copper, so add more lime until the coating stops appearing.
Use only copper, wooden or plastic vessels, not other metals.

safety.text: General safety advice, not from the sources: wear gloves, a mask and eye protection, keep children and animals away, and wash your hands after spraying.
